question: Can a smoothly broken power-law family extrapolate neural-network performance across monotone, non-monotone, and sharp-transition regimes more reliably than previously used single-regime scaling laws?

key_findings.claim: The proposed BNSL is a flexible univariate family of smoothly connected power-law segments that can express asymptotes, slope changes, sharp or gradual breaks, inflection points, and non-monotonic behavior.
key_findings.evidence: The function has an offset, an initial power exponent, and for every break a location, sharpness, and change in exponent. The authors prove that common M1-M3 forms cannot express either non-monotonicity or linear-axis inflection points and that M4 remains monotone, while BNSL can express both.

key_findings.claim: On the two tabulated benchmark domains, BNSL is the best tested form for most, but not all, held-out extrapolation tasks.
key_findings.evidence: Using RMSLE on the scaling-law benchmark, BNSL has the lowest error for 69.44% of downstream vision tasks and 75% of language tasks. It therefore loses on 30.56% and 25% respectively, despite having greater flexibility than the M1-M4 baselines.

anchors.section: Appendix A.36, Acknowledged poor Caltech extrapolations

key_findings.claim: The breadth of the evaluation is mostly breadth of reused curves rather than a single controlled prospective scaling experiment.
key_findings.evidence: The paper fits points taken from published tables and figures across vision, language, RL, retrieval, alignment, robustness, robotics, sparsity, quantization, and other domains, typically holding out one or a few largest x-values. The controlled four-digit-addition study is the main new experiment and averages more than 1000 seeds per dataset size, but it uses one small one-block transformer and dataset sizes 144-1008.

key_findings.claim: BNSL cannot in general forecast a sufficiently sharp future break before observations reach the neighborhood of that break, even with noiseless data and infinitely many replications.
key_findings.evidence: In the four-digit addition simulation, fitting remains inaccurate until the maximum observed dataset size reaches about 415, essentially the break location. The paper concludes that no current method can extrapolate behavior after an additional sufficiently sharp break far beyond the fitted range.

key_findings.claim: The function's success does not by itself establish a universal mechanism or identifiable law, because with enough breaks it can approximate any smooth univariate curve and break selection/cropping adds modeling discretion.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly note universal smooth univariate approximation. They choose the number of breaks by a validation holdout and describe optional cropping of earlier points when sharp old breaks do not help extrapolation; the reported comparison does not apply an explicit complexity penalty or matched-parameter baseline family.

method.core_idea: Replace a single power-law scaling curve by a differentiable sequence of power-law regimes whose break locations, slope changes, and transition widths are learned from smaller-scale observations.
method.mechanism: Fit the BNSL parameters with a brute-force initialization followed by nonlinear least squares in log-error space, choose the number of breaks using held-out large fitting points, and evaluate by extrapolating to still larger held-out observations. Aggregate examples from many published scaling datasets and run a high-replication synthetic arithmetic study for a sharp break.
assumptions: The future curve remains in the same learned regime or begins a transition close enough to the observed range to identify it.
A single scalar scale variable captures the relevant variation despite changes in architecture, data mixture, optimization, and evaluation protocol.
The chosen number of breaks, parameter initialization, bounds, and optional cropping do not overfit the validation/held-out geometry.
Digitized or tabulated points from heterogeneous prior work are accurate and comparable enough for extrapolation conclusions.
RMSLE is appropriate across metrics with different natural noise, floors, and practical costs.

techniques.role: Connects multiple approximately linear log-log regimes with differentiable soft transitions.
Separately represents where a transition happens, how much the exponent changes, and how abrupt it is.
Fits parameters to proportional rather than raw-scale error after a brute-force initialization.
Tests one-step or limited-range extrapolation beyond smaller observed scales.
Separates sampling noise from the intrinsic impossibility of discovering an unseen sharp regime change.

evaluations.setting: Scaling-law benchmark covering downstream vision and upstream/downstream language curves from multiple model families and dataset sizes.
evaluations.metric: Root mean squared logarithmic error on held-out larger-scale points and fraction of tasks on which each functional form has the lowest error.
evaluations.result: BNSL wins 69.44% of downstream image-classification curves and 75% of language curves, while showing conspicuous failures on some Caltech101, BIG-Bench, and other cases.
evaluations.baseline: M1 pure power law, M2 power law plus floor, M3 shifted power law plus floor, and Alabdulmohsin et al.'s M4 saturating form.

evaluations.setting: Published scaling curves spanning RL, diffusion, video, retrieval, sparsity, robustness, coding, calibration, RLHF, robotics, quantization, distillation, molecules, fairness, test-time compute, audio, and multimodal contrastive learning.
evaluations.metric: Visual and occasional RMSLE agreement on one or a few held-out largest-scale observations.
evaluations.result: The fitted family can represent and often extend many diverse curve shapes, but the appendix is primarily a collection of selected case studies rather than a preregistered, uniformly scored benchmark with uncertainty calibration.
evaluations.baseline: Published data trends and, only for subsets, prior functional forms.

evaluations.setting: A one-layer transformer trained on four-digit addition at dataset sizes 144-1008, with more than 1000 seeds per size, plus a noiseless simulation of its fitted BNSL.
evaluations.metric: Test cross-entropy and ability to extrapolate the post-break curve as the maximum fitted dataset size increases.
evaluations.result: BNSL captures the sharp transition only after data reach its neighborhood; the noiseless experiment shows this delay is an identifiability limit, not merely seed noise.
evaluations.baseline: Prior monotone forms that cannot express the linear-axis inflection and a noiseless version of the same broken curve.

limitations: For n breaks the family has 3 + 3n parameters and can approximate any smooth univariate function, yet the headline comparisons do not complexity-match baselines or report information-criterion/Bayesian penalties.
Break-count selection, optional cropping, bounds, and brute-force initialization create researcher degrees of freedom; it is not clear that every appendix curve follows one frozen automated protocol.

Many evaluations hold out only one or a few adjacent largest x-values and reuse points from others' figures, which tests interpolation-like local continuation more often than genuinely remote prospective forecasting.
The benchmark deliberately presents regions around fitted breaks, creating selection toward curves the proposed family is designed to express.
The paper reports root standard log error rather than calibrated predictive intervals and does not quantify parameter non-identifiability or the probability of catastrophic extrapolation failure.
BNSL is not best on 30.56% of vision tasks or 25% of language tasks in the tabulated benchmark, and several plotted failures are explained post hoc as insufficient points near a break.
A univariate curve omits the joint effects of parameters, tokens, compute, data composition, hyperparameters, model family, and post-training interventions.
The form cannot predict a genuinely unseen sharp transition, which sharply limits its use for forecasting novel dangerous capabilities before evidence of the transition appears.
Later work shows that some apparent emergent breaks arise from discontinuous metrics rather than underlying capability changes, so a good broken fit can model an evaluation artifact.
failure_modes: The fitter invents a break to absorb seed noise and extrapolates the spurious new slope far beyond observed data.
A real additional break occurs after the fitted range and invalidates an otherwise precise projection without warning.
Different initializations or break counts yield nearly identical in-range loss but radically different asymptotes and future predictions.
Accuracy or pass/fail metrics manufacture a sharp transition from smoothly improving probabilities.
Architecture, data mixture, optimizer, or post-training changes are encoded as a supposed universal scale transition.
RMSLE rewards a flexible fit on many low-consequence points while hiding a small number of high-consequence catastrophic forecast errors.
A held-out point is close enough to the fit boundary to look predictable, but extrapolation over the actual deployment scale fails.
reusable_insights: Model slope changes explicitly instead of assuming one power law across every scale, but penalize each additional break.
Treat an unseen-break forecast as an abstention region; no curve family can infer an arbitrary sharp transition from a perfectly flat prefix.
Use continuous proper metrics alongside thresholded task success to separate capability change from measurement artifacts.
Bootstrap across seeds and refit across break counts to report predictive distributions, not only a best curve.
Evaluate extrapolators prospectively on frozen protocols with multiple distance horizons and count catastrophic failures.
Jointly model compute, data, model size, family efficiency, and post-training when those factors vary rather than collapsing them onto one x-axis.
open_questions: How often do BNSL break locations and asymptotes remain identifiable under realistic numbers of noisy training runs?
Does BNSL retain an advantage under nested cross-validation, matched model complexity, and genuinely prospective preregistered forecasts?
Can a Bayesian change-point version produce calibrated probability of an unseen future break rather than a point estimate?
Which apparent breaks survive replacement of accuracy and exact-match scores with continuous token- or option-level metrics?
How should multivariate scaling, data mixtures, architecture changes, and post-training interventions be integrated without exploding parameter count?
What forecast horizon and failure probability make a scaling law useful for safety decisions rather than descriptive curve fitting?

competitive_landscape.title: Revisiting Neural Scaling Laws in Language and Vision
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest contemporary benchmark and saturating functional-form alternative.
competitive_landscape.difference: Alabdulmohsin et al. introduce the M4 form and the benchmark reused by the target, emphasizing random-guess and irreducible-error limits. BNSL wins more benchmark curves by adding arbitrary slope changes and non-monotonicity, at the cost of extra parameters and model-selection burden.

competitive_landscape.title: Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later direct critique of interpreting sharp evaluation breaks as emergent capabilities.
competitive_landscape.difference: Schaeffer et al. show that discontinuous metrics and weak statistics can manufacture apparent emergence and that continuous metrics often scale smoothly. BNSL can accurately fit such breaks but does not determine whether they reflect a mechanistic capability transition or a metric artifact.

competitive_landscape.title: Observational Scaling Laws and the Predictability of Language Model Performance
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later alternative for forecasting complex and agentic performance across public model families.
competitive_landscape.difference: Ruan et al. infer a low-dimensional capability space and family-specific compute efficiency from roughly 100 public models, predicting sigmoidal emergent and intervention effects. BNSL instead fits each metric independently as an unconstrained univariate broken curve and cannot share structure across tasks or families.

competitive_landscape.title: A Hitchhiker's Guide to Scaling Law Estimation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later large-scale methodological study of scaling-law estimation and uncertainty drivers.
competitive_landscape.difference: Choshen et al. estimate more than 1000 laws over 485 models and find benefits from intermediate checkpoints, similar-sized references, and repeated small-model seeds. Those findings supply protocol and variance controls largely absent from BNSL's heterogeneous case-study evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: Pretraining Scaling Laws for Generative Evaluations of Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later current work focused on predicting generative pass-at-k evaluations and parameter stability over scale.
competitive_landscape.difference: Schaeffer et al. compare compute, parameter-plus-token, and gold-solution-likelihood laws and study when their parameters stabilize across orders of magnitude. BNSL is more shape-flexible across arbitrary metrics but does not exploit generative-evaluation structure or systematically diagnose stabilization before extrapolation.

novelty_assessment: BNSL's genuine contribution is a memorable, interpretable parameterization that substantially broadens scaling-law expressivity and an unusually wide empirical demonstration that simple power laws often miss regime changes. Its strongest scientific result is the negative one: a sharp unseen future break is not identifiable from pre-break data. Claims of a near-universal predictive law are weaker because the family is a flexible smooth-curve approximator, model selection is discretionary, most evaluations are retrospective local holdouts, and later work supplies both metric-artifact critiques and more structured observational alternatives.
reviewer_notes: Read all 38 extracted pages, including the derivations, tabulated per-task errors, every appendix case study, fitting and break-selection protocol, arithmetic hyperparameters, failure examples, and references. Direct contemporary and later competitors through 2025 were checked against primary arXiv records on 2026-08-23.
